transcript: Let's talk about the British mega musical that arrived too late, left very soon, and also wasn't British. Josh Rosen posted about the mega flop Broadway musical Doctor Zhivago and asked if anyone could share their experiences seeing the show. So here you go! and let's call this another episode of my series Overthinking Theatre Throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history. So like Josh said in his video, Doctor Zhivago played on Broadway in 2015 very briefly, with only 26 previews and 23 regular performances. And I think it still holds my personal record for the shortest open run on Broadway that I personally managed to catch. This was one of many musicals to use the classic side-step maneuver where it was technically based on the original novel, not the 1965 movie. But as always, they made it very obvious that they were trying to ride off the success of the movie. They even included the original song from the film, “Somewhere My Love,” even though it “wasn't based on it.” But what did I actually think of the show? Well, the answer is: not a whole lot. It didn't strike me as a trainwreck, probably not as bad as its mega-flop status would lead you to believe, but it just felt very hollow and unimaginative and kind of dated. The music was written by Lucy Simon, who also did the Secret Garden musical, which I love, and her score from Doctor Zhivago. superficially had this sweepingly beautiful quality, but none of it was at all memorable, either melodically or dramatically. Likewise, the story engaged me enough at the time. Like, I wasn't bored, it just left no impression on me. I really couldn't bring myself to care about anyone or anything on stage. And yet it was so dramatic and kind of just incessantly bombastic, which ended up making it feel kind of unearned and exhausting. And as I hinted out at the beginning of the video, it was very conspicuously trying to emulate the mega musicals that were coming over from the UK In the 80s and 90s. But it didn't manage to find a voice or identity of its own within that style. At the time, I even went so far as to say that it felt like a step backward for musical theater: reheating the nachos of a bygone era. Ironically, though, I can't help but wonder if it might have been received a little better if it opened today. Not necessarily by general audiences. I think it would have struggled to stay afloat commercially regardless. but maybe it would have garnered a bit of a cult fan base from people who are now yearning for more of these large scale musicals again. by contrast, the 2010s on Broadway was an era where artsy musicals from off Broadway were dominating the conversation. Even still, I can't say that it was much of a spectacle. I mean, it was big for sure, but not especially beautiful or impressive. They made heavy use of an LED backdrop, which I was already tired of seeing, even back then. But there was one aspect of this otherwise unmemorable show that managed to cut through the noise, and that was the excellent performance from Paul Alexander Nolan. He played the supporting role of Pasha, a student revolutionary, and he just had this charm and charisma that was such a breath of fresh air every time he came on stage, just injecting a shot of energy into this show that was otherwise kind of dour and stodgy.
